These pages walk through Philip Tagg's book *Everyday Tonality II: Towards a Tonal Theory of What Most People Hear* (2014) in plain words. Tagg's point: most of the music people hear every day (pop, rock, film, games, folk) does not follow the rules of classical harmony, and needs its own words. Page numbers point to the book. The summaries were drafted with AI help from the book's text; check a page before quoting it. New words: [glossary](tagg-glossary.qmd).

## Chapter 5: Melody (pp. 179–203)

Tagg asks what makes a line of notes sound like a melody. His answer: a melody is one line of notes (monodic) that people can easily recognise and sing back. It fits the length of a breath, moves at about the speed of slow to medium speech, flows smoothly, has a clear shape and rhythm, uses a fairly simple set of notes, moves mostly by steps, and rarely spans more than an octave (pp. 179–180). Riffs are often too short and rap is not clearly tuned, though a few riffs are very singable.

He then shows how to describe melodies. By pitch contour: rising, falling, tumbling, V-shaped, arched, wavy and so on. But contour is not enough. The set of notes used, the rhythm, the loudness, the instrument, the language of the words and the phrasing all change a melody's character. Changing Axel F from short, punchy notes to smooth long ones makes it sound like a different kind of music (p. 187).

He also covers repetition patterns (reiteration, sequence, inversion and more) and mood-based types of melody such as "Dream", "Supermusic" (heroic film and TV themes) and "Recitation". Finally he discusses melisma, many notes sung on one syllable, which people hear as emotional singing.


### Key ideas
- Melody means a singable, breath-length line of tones that stands in front of the accompaniment (pp. 179–180).
- Melodies are described by pitch contour: rising, falling, tumbling, V-shaped, centric, terraced, oscillatory, arched, wavy (p. 183).
- Tonal vocabulary, rhythm, dynamics, timbre, phrasing, language and recurring patterns all matter as much as contour (pp. 185–188).
- Body movement and the rhythm of speech shape melodic rhythm: work songs, dances, and the "Scotch snap" in English (pp. 188–189).
- Recurrence patterns include reiteration, recapitulation, sequence, inversion, anaphora, epistrophe and "ready-steady-go" (pp. 193–196).
- A melisma is a smooth string of notes on one syllable; it is often heard as emotional and came into pop through gospel and Anglo-American folk singing (pp. 199–202).

**Example pieces the chapter uses**
- Satisfaction (Rolling Stones) and Layla (Derek and the Dominoes): singable riffs (p. 180).
- Beatles' Yesterday: wavy contour; Can't Buy Me Love: tumbling (pp. 184–185).
- Star Wars and Superman themes: "Supermusic" (pp. 197–198). Blowing in the Wind (Dylan): "Recitation" (p. 198).
- So Emotional (Whitney Houston): pentatonic melismas (p. 202).


### Try this
Pick five songs you know. For each, hum the shape of the chorus and decide which contour type it is. Then pick one tune and sing it first very smoothly, then very short and punchy, and say how its character changes. Finally, listen for a melisma in a current pop song and count the notes sung on one syllable.

## Chapter 6: Polyphony (pp. 205–217)

Polyphony means "many sounds". Tagg uses the word in a wide sense: any time two or more sounds are heard together, or (tonal polyphony) two or more clearly different pitches sound together. He rejects the narrow school-history meaning (European music of about 1400 to 1650), because under his wider meaning a pop band with bass, guitar and drums is polyphonic too (pp. 205–206).

He then sorts out four main kinds. A drone is a note that keeps sounding, as in bagpipes. Heterophony is when several people play or sing the same tune at once, each decorating it a bit differently. Homophony is when all the parts move in the same rhythm at the same time, as in a hymn. Counterpoint is when the lines clearly differ in melody or rhythm.

The key lesson is that homophony and counterpoint are not either/or. A piece is more or less contrapuntal. Most pop and rock mixes both: the singers move together while the bass, drums and riffs do their own thing (p. 213). This helps you listen to a mix and pick out the layers.


### Key ideas
- Polyphony means two or more different sounds at once; tonal polyphony means different pitches (pp. 205–206).
- Arpeggios on guitar or piano are heard as one chord, not as a melody (p. 206).
- A drone is a note held or repeated at one pitch as a reference point for the other parts (pp. 207–208).
- Heterophony is the same melody played at once with small differences, common in the Eastern Mediterranean and Arab world (p. 210).
- Homophony means parts moving in the same rhythm together; counterpoint means lines that differ; the two are matters of degree (pp. 212, 215).
- Pop counterpoint usually appears as call and response overlapping, or as a melody, a lead part and a bass line interacting (p. 215).

**Example pieces the chapter uses**
- The House Of The Rising Sun (Animals) and Your Song (Elton John): arpeggiated keyboard figures (p. 207).
- Old 100th and Martyrdom: homophonic hymns (p. 212).
- Fernando (Abba): homophonic voices plus contrapuntal bass and flute (pp. 213–214).
- Please Mr. Postman (Marvelettes): call and response overlap; Satisfaction (Rolling Stones): melody, lead guitar and bass (p. 216).


### Try this
Listen to a full-band song through headphones. Follow the bass for one chorus, then the drums, then the vocal. Decide: do these parts move in the same rhythm (homophonic) or differently (contrapuntal)? Rate the song on a scale from "very homophonic" to "very contrapuntal".

## Chapter 7: Chords (pp. 219–244)

This is a reference chapter: it teaches the naming system used in the rest of Tagg's book. A chord is two or more different notes sounding together. Chords with two notes are dyads, three notes triads, four tetrads and five pentads (p. 219). The chords here are tertial: built by stacking thirds (every other note of a scale). There are four kinds of tertial triad: major, minor, augmented and diminished (p. 222).

Two systems name chords. Roman numerals are "relative": they tell you which step of the scale the chord is built on, so they work in any key (I, ii, IV, V and so on). Lead-sheet shorthand is "absolute": C always means a C major chord, and extras such as m, 7, maj7, 9, sus4 or add9 are added after the letter in a set order (pp. 220, 235). Lead sheets began in the USA in the 1920s as copyright papers, and guitarists and bass players later used them to play from (pp. 229–230).

For a pop listener this is the "language" for talking about chord progressions such as I–V–vi–IV, or the aeolian cadence ♭VI–♭VII–i. Tagg also notes that lead sheets often leave out inversions and details that you must hear by ear (p. 241).


### Key ideas
- A chord is two or more different notes at once; unisons and octaves do not count (p. 219).
- Tertial triads stack two thirds; major = major third + minor third, minor = minor third + major third (pp. 220, 222).
- Roman numerals are relative and work in any key; capital letters mean major, lower-case mean minor (pp. 220–221).
- Lead-sheet shorthand is absolute and built in a fixed order: root, triad type, seventh, extensions, altered fifth, extras, inversion (p. 235).
- A plain 7 means a flat (minor) seventh; a major seventh must be marked maj or Δ (p. 236).
- Inversions: root position, first inversion (third in the bass) and second inversion (fifth in the bass); shorthand uses a slash, e.g. C/E (pp. 225, 240–241).
- Lead-sheet shorthand cannot properly describe quartal (stacked-fourths) harmony (p. 244).

**Example pieces the chapter uses**
- Sweet Home Alabama (Lynyrd Skynyrd) and Hey Jude (Beatles): the I–♭VII–IV loop (p. 224).
- Satisfaction (Rolling Stones): sus4 chord in the main riff (p. 229).
- Purple Haze (Hendrix): the +9 chord (p. 227).
- Hello (Lionel Richie): dominated by an Am add9 chord that published sheet music left out (p. 242).


### Try this
Choose a song with three or four chords (for example Hey Jude or Sweet Home Alabama). Write its chords as letters in one key, then write the same chords as Roman numerals. Transpose the letters into another key and check that the Roman numerals stay the same.

## Words from these chapters

**Counterpoint**: Polyphony in which the lines clearly differ in melody and/or rhythm. It is the opposite of homophony, though music is only more or less contrapuntal. (Tagg p. 214–215)

**Drone**: A note that sounds at the same pitch throughout all or part of a piece, acting as a reference for the other parts; bagpipes are the classic example. (Tagg p. 207–208)

**Homophony**: Polyphony where the parts move in the same rhythm at the same time, like a hymn. (Tagg p. 212)

**Lead sheet**: A page with the melody, chord symbols and lyrics of a song; the chord symbols are called lead-sheet chord shorthand and name chords in absolute terms (C, Dm7, G7). (Tagg p. 229–230)

**Melisma**: Several smooth, joined notes sung to one syllable. It is the opposite of syllabic singing (one note per syllable) and is heard as emotional. (Tagg p. 199)

**Pitch contour**: The overall shape a melody draws as it goes up and down, for example rising, falling, arched or wavy. (Tagg p. 183)

**Polyphony**: Music in which two or more sounds, or in the tonal sense two or more different pitches, are heard at the same time. (Tagg p. 205–206)

**Tertial**: Describes chords built by stacking thirds, as in common major and minor triads. It is different from quartal harmony, built on fourths. (Tagg p. 219–220)
